findings.finding: Double network probe on the unreachable-remote path: `ensure_store_mounted_best_effort` calls `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` (probe #1, blocks for the probe timeout), returns False, then the per-arm `ensure_initialized` calls `_create_tracker` → `pending_init_attaches_to_existing` (probe #2) before reaching the 'not initialized' error. Two sequential probes each blocking for the full probe timeout doubles user-visible latency on the P1 failure path.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Acknowledge and evaluate `_ref_lock._remote_ref_absent()` as prior art for the advertisement probe; either reuse/extract it as a shared utility or explicitly justify why `init.py` needs its own independent copy.
evidence: Plan: 'Add one shared remote-branch probe used by both _mount_or_create_branch and pending_init_attaches_to_existing whenever neither a local branch nor a local remote-tracking ref exists.'
_ref_lock.py line 301–330: `_remote_ref_absent()` uses `git ls-remote --exit-code` with identical 0/2/other logic and identical fail-closed semantics for non-0/2 returns.
ABSENCE: The plan contains no mention of `_ref_lock.py`, `_remote_ref_absent`, or reuse of the existing probe.
findings.finding: The plan describes adding 'one shared remote-branch probe' using `git ls-remote --exit-code` as if it is new, but `_ref_lock.py` already contains `_remote_ref_absent()` — an essentially identical function using the same command, the same three-outcome exit-code logic (0/2/other), and the same fail-closed semantics for transport errors. The plan does not reference or propose reusing this prior art, meaning the implementation would produce two independent probes with the same semantics that diverge over time.
findings.location: Implementation plan, bullet 2: 'Add one shared remote-branch probe'; src/rebar/_engine/rebar_reconciler/_ref_lock.py lines 301–330
scenarios: Implementer writes a second `_probe_remote_branch()` in `init.py` unaware of `_remote_ref_absent()`, creating two independent probes with divergent timeout handling, warning formats, and future maintainability surface.

AC8 ('Behavioral wiring tests monkeypatch the one shared probe') becomes ambiguous: should they monkeypatch the new probe or the existing `_remote_ref_absent`? If the new probe is a copy, the test seam in `_ref_lock.py` is never exercised by init tests.
findings.suggested_fix: Extract `_remote_ref_absent` (or a generalization of it) into `rebar._store.gitutil` or a new `rebar._commands._git_probe` leaf so both `init.py` and `_ref_lock.py` share the single implementation. The plan's AC8 ('a second independent remote-existence predicate would fail the tests') then enforces this by construction.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Document an explicit back-out / expand-contract path: either (a) describe how to revert to fail-open behavior (e.g. a feature flag, a version-boundary note, or a documented git-revert procedure) or (b) stage the change as 'warn in vX, fail-closed in vX+1' so consumers have a migration window.
evidence: "Never create an orphan unless the override was supplied."
"The override applies only when remote reachability cannot be established."
ABSENCE: no section describes how to revert the deployment if the new fail-closed behavior breaks an unconsidered legitimate use case.
findings.finding: The plan changes a load-bearing default behavior — orphan-bootstrap when no local refs exist — from fail-open to fail-closed, which breaks any consumer (e.g. CI pipelines, air-gapped init scripts) currently relying on the old behavior. The plan offers `--force-new-store` as a migration escape valve but never describes a back-out / rollback plan for the code change itself, nor an expand-contract sequence (e.g., emit a warning in the current release and harden in the next). T4 requires the remedy to be a rollback/back-out plan or expand-contract, not acknowledgement plus a flag alone.
findings.location: Implementation Plan bullet 5 ('fail closed with a distinct error'); bullet 6 ('--force-new-store'); title ('fail closed instead of orphan-bootstrapping')
scenarios: An air-gapped CI job that previously relied on implicit offline orphan-bootstrap starts failing after upgrade. The operator doesn't know about `--force-new-store` until they read the (possibly not-yet-updated) docs. There is no documented procedure to temporarily revert to the old behavior short of a code rollback.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an ADR or AGENTS.md entry documenting the dual-timeout shared-runner seam: why the probe and fetch use different timeouts, what each contract guarantees, and under what conditions each is invoked.
evidence: 'Generalize the existing bounded Git-network seam so _git_fetch retains its 300-second cold-fetch contract and a new advertisement probe uses a short named timeout.'
Files section lists only init.py, _lib_writes.py, init.txt, cli-reference.md, and tests — no ADR or AGENTS.md.
findings.finding: The plan introduces a new architectural seam — a shared network runner with two distinct named timeouts (300 s cold-fetch contract and a short probe timeout) — but lists no ADR, AGENTS.md update, or design-doc entry for this decision. Future maintainers modifying either timeout or the runner will have no record of why the split exists or what the contracts are.
findings.location: Implementation plan (first bullet) and Files section
scenarios: A developer later changes the probe timeout without realising it's a distinct contract from the fetch timeout, silently breaking fail-closed guarantees.
Onboarding reviewers cannot determine why two timeout values exist or what each is responsible for.
findings.suggested_fix: Create `docs/adr/NNN-fail-closed-init-network-seam.md` (or an equivalent section in AGENTS.md) covering: (1) rationale for splitting cold-fetch (300 s) from advertisement probe (short timeout), (2) the three exit-code semantics of `git ls-remote --exit-code`, (3) the deliberate-bootstrap override contract. Reference this doc from the implementation-plan bullet.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either expose the probe timeout as a configurable value (env var, config key, or CLI option) or explicitly document in the plan that the short timeout is intentionally fixed and state the chosen value with its rationale.
evidence: 'a new advertisement probe uses a short named timeout'
No mention of the timeout being exposed in project configuration, environment variables, or CLI flags.
findings.finding: The advertisement probe's 'short named timeout' is specified only as a named constant, not as a user-configurable or environment-configurable value. Networks in slow CI, corporate proxies, or constrained edge environments may time out the probe faster than intended, causing spurious fail-closed errors that the operator cannot remedy without a code change.
findings.location: Implementation plan, first bullet; AC line about 'short bound'
scenarios: CI running over a slow link fails every `rebar init` because the probe timeout is hard-coded to a value too short for that environment.
An operator on a satellite link cannot override the probe timeout without patching source.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `REBAR_PROBE_TIMEOUT` environment variable (defaulting to the chosen short value, e.g., 10 s) and thread it through the shared runner, consistent with how `_FETCH_TIMEOUT = 300` is already a named constant. Document the default and the env var in init.txt and the ADR.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a one-sentence positive rationale for the `--force-new-store` scope boundary (e.g. 'scoped to unreachable-only because allowing it to override a known-advertised branch would recreate the P1 data-loss scenario even when the operator explicitly requests it').
evidence: Plan states the scoping rule but not WHY this boundary exists

The ticket root cause (P1 01e8-302b) shows that the original bug was exactly 'fetch timed out → fell back to orphan bootstrap' — if --force-new-store could override a fetch failure, an operator could accidentally re-trigger the original P1 with the new flag
findings.finding: The plan provides no positive rationale for why `--force-new-store` is deliberately scoped to the 'remote unreachable' case only and explicitly excluded from overriding an 'advertised + fetch-failed' scenario. This design choice protects against accidental orphan-bootstrap over a real remote branch when fetch is merely slow, but without a stated rationale the implementer may not understand the boundary and may inadvertently allow the flag to override fetch failures too.
findings.location: Implementation plan: '`--force-new-store` ... The override applies only when remote reachability cannot be established; it does not override an advertised branch or a failed fetch of one.'
scenarios: An implementer reading only the plan (not the ticket) may not understand why fetch-failure is not overridable and may be tempted to relax the boundary 'for convenience', reintroducing the P1 via the new flag.
